questions.q: Muhammad Ghori granted first Iqta in India to –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Soon after Ghori’s victories, the Iqta system was established in North India. In India, Muhammad Ghori granted the first Iqta to Qutbuddin Aibak. From 1192 to 1206 AD, Aibak administered the conquered parts of North India as Ghori’s representative. During this period, Aibak also expanded Turkish power in North India.

questions.q: Muhammad Ghori was defeated by the Chaulukyas of Gujarat in
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Muhammad Ghori attacked Gujarat in 1178 AD. At that time, the Anhilwad Chalukya ruler of Gujarat was Mularaja II. Naika Devi, the widowed mother of Mularaja II, acted as his guardian and led the Chalukya (Solanki) army against Ghori. Near Mount Abu, on the field of Kasahrada, the Chalukya/ Solanki army defeated Muhammad Ghori. This was Ghori’s first defeat in India. Some sources also mention this invasion (1178 AD) during the reign of Bhima II. This confusion probably arises because Mularaja II’s reign ended in 1178 AD and Bhima II’s reign began in the same year. However, most historians accept Mularaja II as the Chalukya/Solanki ruler of Gujarat at the time of Ghori’s invasion (1178 AD).

questions.q: Who was the first ruler of the Slave Dynasty?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The first ruler of the Slave Dynasty in India was Qutbuddin Aibak (1206–1210 AD). He belonged to a Turkish tribe called Aibak. In childhood, he was purchased as a slave by Qazi Fakhruddin Abdul Aziz Kufi of Nishapur. The Qazi took proper care of him and ensured that he received complete education. Aibak recited the Quran in a very melodious voice; therefore, he became famous as Quran-khwan (one who recites the Quran). Later, he was brought from Nishapur to Ghazni, where Ghori purchased him. Due to his talent, dedication, and honesty, Aibak soon gained Ghori’s trust. Ghori promoted him to the post of Amir-e-Akhur, and from there a new chapter of his life began. He was the first Turkish ruler of Delhi, although he ruled from Lahore. Aibak never formally assumed the title of Sultan. He remained content with the titles of Malik and Sipahsalar. After receiving a deed of manumission from Ghiyasuddin, Ghori’s successor, Aibak was officially freed from slavery in 1208 AD.

questions.q: The capital of Qutbuddin Aibak was:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: After the death of Muhammad Ghori (1206 AD), the notable people and amirs of Lahore invited Qutb-ud-din Aibak to assume sovereign powers. Therefore, he went to Lahore, assumed power, and was formally enthroned in 1206 AD. Aibak’s capital was Lahore. After ascending the throne, Aibak’s biggest challenge came from Taj-ud-din Yalduz and Nasir-ud-din Qubacha—Ghori’s slaves and successors/ claimants to his territories. Aibak married his daughter to Qubacha and thus brought him to his side; however, the threat from Yalduz continued. This is why Aibak always stayed in Lahore. He never got an opportunity to go to Delhi.

questions.q: The Muslim ruler whose empire was regarded as a part of Dar-ul-Islam was
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: During the reign of Iltutmish, in 1229 AD, the Caliph of Baghdad bestowed a robe of honour (khilat) upon him. Now the Sultanate, in theory, became a part of Dar-ul-Islam under the Caliph of Baghdad.

questions.q: Iltutmish appointed his first Subedar in Bihar to :
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Iltutmish captured Bihar Sharif and Barh, and near Teliyagarhi (close to the Rajmahal hills) a minor skirmish took place between Hisam-ud-din Aiwaz and the royal army. According to Minhaj, ultimately a treaty was concluded between the two sides. Iltutmish appointed Malik Jani as the Subedar of Bihar in place of Aiwaz.

questions.q: "His theory of kingship was based on the principles of prestige, power and justice." Who said these words about Balban?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above / More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Dr. R.P. Tripathi, in his book 'Some Aspects of Muslim Administration', while explaining Balban’s concept of kingship, stated that “His theory of kingship was based on the principles of prestige, power and justice.” For this conclusion regarding Balban’s kingship, he used as his basis the description presented by Zia-ud-din Barani on Balban’s theory of kingship. Probably for this reason, in its preliminary and final answer keys, the Bihar Public Service Commission has accepted option (b) as correct.

questions.q: Who was the first Muslim ruler to formulate the 'Theory of Kingship' similar to the 'Theory of divine right of the kings'?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Balban was the first Muslim ruler who propounded the theory of kingship on the lines of the theory of divine right of kings. According to this, the Sultan is the representative of God on earth (niyabat-e-khudai), and his position comes after the Prophet. The king is zill-e-Allah or zill-e-ilahi, i.e., the reflection of God. He said to his son Bughra Khan—“The office of the Sultan is the living symbol of absolutism.”

questions.q: The term Zillillah was first used by
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Balban was the first Muslim ruler who propounded the theory of kingship on the lines of the theory of divine right of kings. According to this, the Sultan is the representative of God on earth (niyabat-e-khudai), and his position comes after the Prophet. The king is zill-e-Allah or zill-e-ilahi, i.e., the reflection of God. He said to his son Bughra Khan—“The office of the Sultan is the living symbol of absolutism.”

questions.q: Which Delhi Sultan is known for adopting the 'blood and iron' policy?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: It is said about Balban that he adopted the policy of “blood and iron.” Two main features of Balban’s theory of kingship were: first, the post of the Sultan is bestowed by God, and second, the Sultan must be absolute. According to him, “The Sultan is God’s representative on earth (niyabat-e-khudai), and his position is after the Prophet. The Sultan receives inspiration and power from God. Therefore, common people or nobles have no right to criticize his actions.”

questions.q: Tughril Khan raised a standard of revolt during whose reign?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: An important revolt during Balban’s reign was the revolt of Tughril Khan. Balban had appointed Tughril Khan as the governor of Bengal, but he declared himself the independent ruler of Bengal, assumed the title of “Sultan Mugisuddin,” issued coins in his own name, and also had the khutba read in his name. To suppress Tughril’s revolt, Balban first sent an army under Amin Khan and thereafter under Bahadur, but both failed. Enraged, Balban advanced towards Bengal along with his son Bughra Khan, but Tughril fled after abandoning his capital. Ultimately, Tughril was captured and killed, and Balban appointed his son Bughra Khan as the iqtadar of Bengal.

questions.q: Who among the following introduced the Persian festival Nouruz in India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban (1266–1287 A.D.) started the practice of celebrating the Iranian festival Nauroz in India. Nauroz is the Iranian New Year, also known as the Persian New Year. Balban also introduced the practices of sijda and paibos in his court, which were imitations of Persian tradition.

questions.q: Who was the first ruler of the Khilji dynasty?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Jalaluddin Khilji founded the Khilji dynasty in 1290 A.D. He had his coronation in 1290 A.D. in the unfinished Kilokhari (Kilughari) palace built by Kaiqubad. According to Dr. A.L. Srivastava, Jalaluddin Khilji was the first Turkish Sultan of Delhi who placed before himself the principle of “liberal despotism.”

questions.q: "Thus to Ala-ud-din belongs the credit of being the first Turkish Sultan of Delhi to bring the church under the control of the state and to usher in factors that might make the state secular in theory." Who wrote these words?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above / More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A.L. Srivastava, in his book The Sultanate of Delhi (711– 1526 A.D.), wrote about Alauddin Khilji: “Alauddin was the first Turkish Sultan of Delhi who was credited with bringing religion under the control of the state and introducing such elements which, in theory, made the state secular.”

questions.q: “When he attained Kingship, he was fully independent of rules and orders of Shariat.” For which Sultan Barani made this statement?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Ziauddin Barani made the above statement for Alauddin Khalji. Alauddin was the first Sultan of Delhi who established state control over religion. Explaining his policy in this context, he himself said that, “I do not know what is right and what is wrong in the eyes of the law. I give orders for whatever I consider suitable for the welfare of the state or for a particular occasion. What will happen to me on the Day of Judgment, I do not know.” Alauddin revived Balban’s idea regarding kingship. He believed in the sovereign authority of the king, who is merely the representative of God on earth. He did not consider it necessary to seek the Caliph’s permission to increase his power; therefore, he made no request to the Caliph for recognition of his position. He described himself as ‘Yamin-ul-Khilafat Nasir Amir-ul- Muminin’. Thus, Alauddin was the first Sultan of Delhi who did not allow religion to interfere in politics. Alauddin remained free from the influence of the ulama.

questions.q: Who among the army-commanders of Alauddin Khilji died fighting against the Mongols?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Alauddin’s famous general Zafar Khan was killed while fighting the Mongols. He was the best and bravest general of his time.

questions.q: Padmini is associated with Ala-ud-Din’s conquest of Chittor. She was the wife of
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The story of Padmini is based on the poetic work ‘Padmavat’, written in 1540 AD by Malik Muhammad Jayasi. According to it, Padmini was the extremely beautiful and learned wife of Rana Ratan Singh of Chittor. Amir Khusro mentioned the love episode of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba in his work, and in his hints he compared Alauddin to Solomon and Padmini to Sheba. Probably on this basis, Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed Padmavat, and the story of Queen Padmini as the queen of Rana Ratan Singh took shape.

questions.q: Who was the ruler of Chittor at the time of Alauddin Khilji’s invasion?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

According to it, Padmini was the extremely beautiful and learned wife of Rana Ratan Singh of Chittor. Probably on this basis, Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed Padmavat, and the story of Queen Padmini as the queen of Rana Ratan Singh took shape.

questions.q: Who was the ruler of Devagiri at the time of Alauddin Khilji’s invasion?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: At the time of Alauddin Khilji’s invasion, Ramchandra Dev was the Yadava dynasty ruler of Devagiri. During Jalaluddin Khilji’s reign, Alauddin Khalji first attacked Devagiri in 1296 AD and forced its ruler Ramchandra Dev to pay an annual tribute. But after Alauddin became the Sultan, when Ramchandra Dev stopped paying the annual tribute, Alauddin, angered by this, sent an army against Devagiri under the leadership of Malik Kafur. In this war, Ramchandra Dev was defeated and he surrendered.

questions.q: During the regime of which Sultan was the Khalisa land developed on a large scale?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The main objective of Alauddin’s revenue and land-tax system was to establish a powerful and autocratic state. He confiscated land from those persons who had received it as milk-idrar, inam, and waqf (land received as a religious/ charitable endowment), etc. As a result, Khalisa land was developed on a large scale.

questions.q: Which Sultan demanded half the crops on land after measurement as revenue?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Alauddin Khilji was the first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate to introduce certain changes in land-revenue policy. He fixed 50% of the produce as land revenue and insisted that it should be collected in the form of grain. Before him, Balban and Iltutmish did not levy land revenue at a rate higher than one-third of the produce. During the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq too, the rate of land tax was 50%, similar to Alauddin’s. Although in this question both options (c) and (d) are correct, the Bihar Public Service Commission, in its final answer key, accepted option (c) as correct.

questions.q: Who was deputed for the conquest of Dwarasamudra by Ala-ud-din Khilji ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Alauddin Khilji appointed Malik Kafur for the conquest of Dwarasamudra. Dwarasamudra was the capital of the Hoysala kingdom, and its ruler was Vira Ballala III. The conquest of most parts of South India is largely credited to Malik Kafur.

questions.q: Nizamuddin Auliya refused to meet which Sultan?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya witnessed the reign of more than seven Sultans who came to power one after another; however, he never went to anyone’s court. Sultan Jalaluddin Khilji was probably the first ruler who, after hearing about the Shaikh’s fame and greatness, offered him a few villages and expressed a desire to meet him. The Shaikh refused, saying: “My khanqah has two doors; if the Sultan enters from one, I will leave from the other.” Later, when Sultan Jalaluddin wished to meet him without prior notice, Auliya’s beloved disciple Amir Khusro informed Auliya about it. As soon as he received the information, Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya immediately left for Ajodhan to visit his spiritual master (Baba Farid). Thus, Auliya continued to avoid meeting the Sultan directly. It is also mentioned that Alauddin Khilji wished to meet Auliya, but no such dramatic incident is associated with Alauddin as is associated with Jalaluddin.

questions.q: Who started the Public Distribution System in the Sultanate period?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khilji started the Public Distribution System

questions.q: Malik Kafur also known as "Hazar Dinari" was bought by whom ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: According to the famous book 'History of Khalijis' written by famous historian K.S.Lal, around 1299 CE, during Alauddin Khilji’s Gujarat campaign, the commander Nusrat Khan attacked the wealthy port of Cambay (Khambhat) and obtained a large amount of gold, silver, jewels, and other valuable items. During the same campaign, the slave Malik Kafur was captured. This was the time when Nusrat Khan seized Malik Kafur from his owner. Since Malik Kafur’s owner had purchased him for one thousand dinars, he came to be called “Hazar-Dinari.” Along with the booty, Nusrat Khan sent Malik Kafur to Delhi to Alauddin. Later, impressed by Kafur’s extraordinary ability and personality, Sultan Alauddin Khilji made him his most trusted commander. The credit for Alauddin’s Deccan campaigns and victories is mainly given to Malik Kafur. From this description, it is clear that Nusrat Khan did not purchase Malik Kafur; rather, he captured him during the Gujarat campaign. Therefore, the closest answer is option (c).

questions.q: Who among the following opposed the power of the Khalifa?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: None of the sultans given in the options opposed the power of the Khalifa. Iltutmish obtained recognition from the Khalifa; however, the Sultan of Bengal, Ghiyasuddin, had also obtained recognition from the Khalifa. By attacking him, Iltutmish, in a way, also challenged the authority of the Khalifa. Alauddin Khilji, Balban, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq were all practically independent rulers, but none of them opposed the power or authority of the Khalifa. Only Mubarak Khilji declared himself the Khalifa and assumed the title Khalifatullah. In this way, he opposed the authority of the Khalifa.

questions.q: Who among the following rulers, ruled for the maximum period?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The reigns of these four rulers of the Delhi Sultanate are estimated to be as follows: Alauddin Khilji – approximately 20 years. Muhammad bin Tughlaq – approximately 26 years. Ghiyasuddin Balban – approximately 20/21 years. Bahlol Lodi, the founder of the Lodi dynasty, reigned approximately 38 years, which is clearly longer than all the other rulers mentioned above.

questions.q: Which one of the following Sultans provided employment to the unemployed?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Firoz Shah Tughlaq carried out some welfare works for the benefit of ordinary people. He opened an office for appointments (employment office) and, after thoroughly examining each person’s qualities and abilities, he appointed as many people as possible and tried to solve the problem of unemployment.

questions.q: Which of the following Sultan had the most number of slaves in his court?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Firoz Tughlaq was very fond of slaves. During his time, the number of slaves possibly reached up to 180,000. For their supervision, a separate department (Diwan-i-Bandagan) was formed, and full attention was given to the education of the slaves.

questions.q: What was ‘Dar-ul-Shafa’ established by Firoz Tughluq?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Firoz Tughlaq was the first Indian ruler who arranged Hajj at the expense of the state. He also established a charitable hospital named Dar-ul-Shafa (also written Dar-ul-Shifa) and appointed skilled physicians (hakims) there.

questions.q: Which one of the following Sultans of Delhi introduced measures for improving the quality of fruits?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Due to his interest in horticulture, Firoz Shah Tughlaq got about 1200 new gardens planted near Delhi, and he also took measures to improve the quality of fruits in those gardens.

questions.q: Which Delhi Sultan built the maximum number of canals?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The reign of Firoz Shah Tughlaq became famous for creating the largest network of canals in India. To provide irrigation facilities, he constructed five major canals. After obtaining the approval of the ulema (religious scholars), Firoz Tughlaq was the first Delhi Sultan to impose an irrigation tax called Haqq-e-Sharb. Farmers who used water from royal canals for irrigation had to pay an additional tax equal to one-tenth of their produce.

questions.q: Which one of the following dynasties ruled over India after the invasion of Timur?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Timur’s invasion (1398 AD) greatly weakened the Delhi Sultanate and the power of the Tughlaq dynasty, and it hastened their decline. With the death of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah in 1412 AD, the Tughlaq dynasty came to an end. In 1413 AD, the nobles chose Daulat Khan as the Sultan of Delhi; however, he was defeated by Khizr Khan. Khizr Khan was the Subahdar (provincial governor) of Multan appointed by Timur. Later, he captured Lahore, Dipalpur, and Upper Sindh. After Timur’s invasion, in 1414 AD, he took control of Delhi and laid the foundation of a new dynasty—the Sayyid dynasty.

questions.q: Which of the following Sultans founded a town where now stands Agra?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: In 1504 AD, Sikandar Lodi founded a new city named Agra on the banks of the Yamuna River with the objective of keeping the rulers of Rajasthan under control, and he made it his capital. He made efforts to promote agriculture and trade. A standard measure called “Gaz-e-Sikandari” was introduced during his time. He arranged free food for the poor. During his reign, a list of capable persons was prepared and presented before him every six months. He was educated and scholarly. On his orders, an Ayurvedic text was translated into Persian and was named “Farhang-e-Sikandari.” During his period, an excellent treatise on vocal music, “Lazzat-e- Sikandarshahi,” was composed. Sikandar Lodi was very fond of listening to the shehnai. He wrote poems under the penname “Gulrukhi.”

questions.q: Who was the founder of the Vijayanagara Empire?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 AD during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq by two brothers, Harihara and Bukka. The capital of this kingdom was Hampi, situated on the banks of the Tungabhadra River.

questions.q: Identify the first ruler of Vijayanagara who captured Goa from the Bahamani’s?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: After Bukka’s death in 1377 AD, his son Harihara II (1377– 1404 AD) ascended the throne and adopted the title “Maharajadhiraja.” He conquered regions like Kanara, Mysore, Tiruchanapalli, Kanchi, etc., and collected tribute from the king of Sri Lanka. He also struggled with the Bahmani kingdom. Harihara II’s greatest achievement was the capture of Goa in the west from the Bahmani state. He was a devotee of Shiva (in the form of Virupaksha).

questions.q: With whom did the king of Vijayanagara, Krishnadeva Raya fought the battle of Golconda?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Vijayanagara king Krishnadeva Raya fought the Golconda war against the Golconda Sultan Quli Qutb Shah. The Qutb Shahi dynasty in Golconda was founded by Quli Qutb Shah. When Krishnadeva Raya was busy in a war with Odisha, Qutb Shah attacked the forts of Pangala and Guntur located on the Vijayanagar frontier and captured forts such as Warangal, Kondavidu, etc. After this, he tried to attack Vijayanagar. A conflict took place between Krishnadeva Raya and Qutb Shah, and the Qutb Shahi army was defeated.

questions.q: What was the chief characteristic of the financial system of the Vijayanagara Empire?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The Vijayanagara state derived income from various sources, such as land revenue, property tax, trade tax, professional tax, taxes imposed on industries, social and community taxes, and fines imposed for crimes. Land was properly surveyed, and 1/6 of the produce was collected as land tax (1/6 as land tax was the ideal rate, but in practice it ranged between 1/6 and 1/3 depending on the productivity of the land). A tax called ‘Shisht’ (land tax) was the chief source of the state’s income. The central revenue department was called ‘Athavane’ (Asthavan or Athvan).

questions.q: The remains of the Vijayanagara Empire are found in?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The ruins of Hampi (located in present-day Karnataka) represent the ancient capital of the Vijayanagara Empire. The famous Virupaksha Temple is located here. Hampi is also included in the UNESCO World Heritage Sites list.

questions.q: Which among the following King's region Persian traveller 'Abdur Razzaq' came to India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq came to Vijayanagara during the reign of Devaraya II of the Sangama dynasty (tenure: 1422–1446 A.D.).

questions.q: Who among the following famous rulers founded a suburban township of Nagalapuram, near Vijayanagara, after his mother's name?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.D: More than one of the above
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529 A.D.) was a ruler of the Tuluva dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire and is considered its most powerful ruler. He founded Nagalambapuram, now known as Nagalapuram, named after his mother Nagalamba. It is located in the Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh.

questions.q: Which famous war took place in 1565 A.D.?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In 1565, in the famous Battle of Talikota, the combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara. In this combined army, Berar alone was not included. According to Firishta, the battle was fought at Talikota, but the actual battlefield lay between two villages named Rakkasi and Tangadi. At the time of the Battle of Talikota, Sadasiva Raya was the ruler of Vijayanagara, but the real power was in the hands of his minister Rama Raya. Rama Raya was a capable commander; he tried to create divisions among the Muslim rulers of the Bahmani states, but he did not succeed. In this very battle, Hussain Nizam Shah personally killed Rama Raya.

questions.q: 'Diwan-i-Arz' department was associated with:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Diwan-i-Arz was the military department of the Sultanate period, and the head of this department was called ‘Ariz-i- Mumalik’. He was responsible for the administration of military affairs. He inspected the military contingents maintained by the iqta-holders.

questions.q: Which of the following indicates taxes levied on the land product? i. Kharaj ii. Khums iii. Ushr iv. Mukta'i Select your answer from the following codes –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Kharaj, Ushr and Muqta’i indicate taxes levied on land produce, whereas Khums was not a tax on land produce; rather, Khums was war booty. Khums was obtained through plunder from the people of the enemy state during war. From this booty, 4/5 was distributed among the soldiers and the remaining 1/5 was deposited in the state treasury; however, Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughlaq deposited 4/5 in the treasury and distributed the remaining 1/5 among the soldiers. Sikandar Lodi did not take any share from buried treasure.

questions.q: Zawabits were concerned with :
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: In the administrative terminology of the Sultanate period, Zawabit was related to state law.

questions.q: During the Delhi Sultanate, the designation 'Muqaddam or Chaudhari' was used for
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.D: More than one of the above
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: During the Delhi Sultanate, the terms ‘Khut’, ‘Muqaddam’, or ‘Chaudhary’ were used for the village headman (sarpanch), who also worked to collect revenue for the Sultanate.

questions.q: Coins-Tanka, Shashgani and Jital of Sultanate period was made of which of the following metals-
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The two major coins of the Sultanate period were Jital and Tanka. Iltutmish was the first Turkish ruler of the Delhi Sultanate to issue pure Arabic coins. His contribution to the currency system was the greatest among the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate because he introduced two major coins— the silver Tanka and the copper Jital. Shashgani was also a silver coin. The ratio of Tanka and Jital was 1 : 48.

questions.q: What is ‘Adhai Din ka Jhonpra’?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Aibak constructed the mosques ‘Quwwat-ul-Islam’ in Delhi and ‘Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra’ in Ajmer. He started the construction of the Qutub Minar in Delhi, which was completed by Iltutmish.

questions.q: The Qutub Minar was completed by-
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The construction of the Qutub Minar was started by Qutbud-din Aibak, and it was completed during the reign of Sultan Iltutmish. It was named ‘Qutub Minar’ after the famous Sufi saint Khwaja Qutb-ud-din Bakhtiyar Kaki. It is a circular, five-storeyed structure. During the reign of Firoz Shah Tughlaq, the fourth storey suffered considerable damage; therefore, Firoz not only reconstructed the fourth storey but also got the fifth storey built. Thus, instead of four storeys, the Qutub Minar came to have five storeys, which still exist today. Sultan Ulugh Khan and Razia Sultan had no contribution to the construction of the Qutub Minar.

questions.q: Which Sultan built Alai Darwaza?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The ‘Alai Darwaza’ was constructed by Sultan Alauddin Khalji near the Qutub Minar. It was built using red sandstone and marble. It was completed in 1311 A.D. Like Iltutmish’s tomb, it has a large square chamber with a dome on the roof, and on each of its four walls there is an arched entrance gateway.

questions.q: Who was the author of Tabaqat-i-Nasiri?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The author of ‘Tabaqat-i-Nasiri’ was Minhaj-us-Siraj, and it was dedicated to Sultan Nasiruddin. This work has 23 chapters. H. G. Raverty translated it into English. This book contains a direct account of Muhammad Ghori’s conquest of India. It is noteworthy that Minhaj stated that Qutbuddin Aibak issued coins in his own name and had the khutba read.

questions.q: The account of the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta is known as
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Ibn Battuta was a resident of Morocco in Africa, who came to Delhi during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq. He wrote his travel account in the Arabic language in a book titled Rihla (Rehla). He criticized the policies of Muhammad Tughlaq’s period.

questions.q: Who composed ‘Barahmasa’?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: ‘Barahmasa’ was composed by Malik Muhammad Jayasi. Among Jayasi’s works—‘Padmavat’, ‘Akharavat’, and ‘Aakhiri Kalam’—‘Padmavat’ holds an important place in Hindi literature.

questions.q: Which great saint wrote the book Gyan Deepak?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.D: More than one of the above
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: Saint Dariya Saheb composed the book titled ‘Gyan Deepak’. He was from Bihar. Salar Masood Ghazi was the head of Mahmud of Ghazni’s army. His dargah is located at Bahraich in Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: “Chach Nama” was translated in to Persian by
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.C: Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Chachnama was translated into Persian by Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi. Chachnama is a book written in the Arabic language. Clear information about the author’s name is not available. Chachnama contains an account of the history of Sindh from 680 to 718 C.E. A complete translation from Persian into English was done in 1900 A.D. by Mirza Kalichbeg Fredunbeg.

questions.q: ''Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi' was written by
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: ‘Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi’ is the title of two separate Persian works written by Shams-e-Siraj Afif and Ziauddin Barani, which have the same title. In the given options, option (a) is the correct answer.

questions.q: Paper came to be used in India in the -:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The first use of paper in India may be considered to have begun approximately during the 7th to 8th centuries. According to available evidence, by the 11th century, documents written on paper began to appear in India, and in the 12th–13th centuries, the use of paper is clearly seen in manuscripts and royal records. In its final answer key, the Bihar Public Service Commission has selected option (a) as the correct option.
questions.note: ⚠ No officially verified answer for this question. BPSC's final answer key selected option (a) '12th century'. Some historical evidence suggests paper use in India may go back further (7th-11th centuries), but this is the officially accepted answer.

chapters.chapter_name: Provincial Dynasties of North India and the Deccan Region

questions.q: Who was the founder of the Bahamani Kingdom?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: As a result of the rebellion of the Amiran-e-Sadah in the Deccan, the Bahmani Empire was established in the last days of Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign. A chief named Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu, 1347–1358 A.D.) assumed the title of “Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah” and ascended the throne in 1347 A.D., thereby laying the foundation of the Bahmani Empire. He made Gulbarga the capital of his newly established empire and named it “Ahsanabad.” For administering the empire, he divided it into four tarafs (provinces)—Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar, and Bidar. Each province was under a governor. The Gulbarga province was the most important, and Bijapur was also included in it. He fought the Hindu rulers of the south and adopted the practice of granting posts and jagirs to his followers. He ordered that jizya should not be collected from Hindus.

questions.q: Shaikh Bahauddin Zakaria belonged to which sect?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In India, the Suhrawardi order began with Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya (1182–1262 A.D.). In this Sufi order, saints like Shaikh Sadruddin Arif, Shaikh Ruknuddin Abul Fath, and Shaikh Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari were notable. The saints of this order emphasized a comfortable life. They did not consider wealth and property as obstacles in spiritual practice.

questions.q: A common feature of all Bhakti Saints was that they –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Composed their verses in the language understood by their followers
options.B: Rejected the authority of the priestly class
options.C: Encouraged women to go to the temples

questions.explanation: The conduct of the saints of the Bhakti movement was very lofty. Many of them travelled widely and met different kinds of people with differing ideas. These saints contributed significantly to the development of the common people’s languages. They greatly aided the growth of Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, etc. Bhakti saints gave their teachings in regional languages so that people could easily listen and understand them. As a result, regional languages developed.

questions.q: Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis made devotional religion popular in
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The Nath-panthis, Siddhas, and Yogis popularized Bhakti religion in North India. They believed that the path to liberation and the attainment of the formless divine is possible through meditation; therefore, they advocated methods like yogic postures, breathing practices, exercise, and meditation as means to attain God.

questions.q: Which of the following Sufi Silsilah was founded in Bihar?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The Firdousia (Firdausi) silsila was established in Bihar. The most prominent Sufi of this silsila in India was Shaikh Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri. Shaikh Maneri was the leading propagator of this silsila in Bihar.

questions.q: Who was the founder of the Mughal dynasty in India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Babur was the founder of the Mughal dynasty. The Mughal rulers were actually from a Turkic branch called Chagatai. This branch was named after the second son of the famous Mongol leader Genghis Khan, who held authority over the Turkistan region of Central Asia.

questions.q: The main reason for Babur’s victory in the battle of Panipat was –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526 between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi, in which Babur won on the strength of his military skill. Although Babur’s army was smaller than Lodi’s, he achieved victory due to his skilled military strategy. Ibrahim Lodi himself was an inexperienced person. Babur writes, “He was an inexperienced man and showed great carelessness in his actions. He advanced and halted without any arrangement, and became absorbed in the struggle without any foresight.”

questions.q: Consider the following statements : The arrival of Babur into India led to the 1. introduction of gunpowder in the subcontinent 2. introduction of arch and dome in the region’s architecture 3. establishment of the Timurid dynasty in the region 4. introduction of cannons in warfare Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.question_type: Multiple Statements — Correct Combination by Code
questions.explanation: As a result of Babur’s arrival, the Timurid dynasty was established in India. Babur was the fifth descendant of Timur from the paternal line. With Babur’s arrival, the use of cannons in warfare began in India. His artillery is regarded as the main factor behind his victory in the First Battle of Panipat. With the help of Turkish gunners named Ustad Ali and Mustafa, he prepared a strong artillery unit. Gunpowder had already reached the Indian subcontinent before Babur came, whereas the use of arches and domes in architecture began only after the arrival of the Turks. Hence, statements 1 and 2 are incorrect, while statements 3 and 4 are correct.

questions.q: Who among the following made an offer to Humayun that he would surrender Bihar and pay an annual tribute of 10 lakh dinars if he was allowed to retain Bengal?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.D: More than one of the above
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: During the Bengal campaign, Sher Khan proposed to Humayun that he would hand over Bihar to Humayun if he was allowed to capture Bengal, and he would also pay an annual tribute of 10 lakh dinars.

questions.q: Who among these rulers divided his troops into units of two hundred, two hundred and fifty and five hundred?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Islam Shah was the son of Sher Shah. Islam Shah ruled over almost the whole of North India for about 8 years, and he died around 1553 AD. Islam Shah divided his military troops into units of 50, 200, 250 and 500. Possibly, this system of military division was also in practice during Sher Shah’s time. It is noteworthy that the Bihar Public Service Commission has considered option (e) as the correct answer.

questions.q: When Humayun invaded Chunar Fort first time ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Humayun attacked Chunar Fort for the first time in 1532 AD. He besieged the fort for four months, after which Sher Khan accepted Humayun’s suzerainty. In addition, in 1531 AD he attacked Kalinjar.

questions.q: Who among the following has constructed a mausoleum for her emperor husband ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Haji Begum had the mausoleum (tomb) of her husband Humayun built in Delhi during 1565–72 A.D. The plan of this mausoleum was prepared by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas (an Iranian architect). This mausoleum is mainly built of red sandstone and white marble. A Charbagh-style garden was laid out for this mausoleum.

questions.q: Arrange properly as per dates of four important battles fought by Humayun, the names of the battlefields are given below –
questions.question_type: Chronological Order — Correct Sequence
questions.explanation: The sequence of the four major battles fought by Humayun is as follows—Deora, Chausa, Kannauj and Sirhind. In 1532 A.D., he defeated the Afghan rebels at a place called Daurah (Deora), situated on the banks of the Gomati River. In 1539 A.D., in the Battle of Chausa, Humayun had to face defeat at the hands of Sher Shah; in this very battle, a water-carrier (bhishti) named Nizam saved Humayun’s life. This victory at Chausa against Humayun enhanced both the power and prestige of Sher Khan (Sher Shah). He assumed the title “Farid al-Din Sher Shah,” got the khutba read in his name, and also had it inscribed on the coins. In 1540 A.D., in the Battle of Kannauj or Bilgram too, Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah and was forced to wander here and there like an exile. In 1555 A.D., the victory in the Battle of Sirhind once again restored Humayun’s lost kingdom to him. Thus, the correct order of the battles is—Deora (1532 A.D.), Chausa (1539 A.D.), Kannauj (1540 A.D.) and Sirhind (1555 A.D.).

questions.q: Which of the following rulers at first assumed the title of ‘Hazrat-e-Ala’ and afterward ‘Sultan’?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: After defeating the Bengal ruler Nusrat Shah, Sher Khan (Sher Shah Suri) assumed the title “Hazrat-e-Ala.” After defeating Humayun in the Battle of Chausa in 1539 A.D., he assumed the title “Sher Shah,” got the khutba read in his name, and had coins minted.

questions.q: Where is Sher Shah’s tomb located ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Sher Shah’s tomb is built at a place called Sasaram in Rohtas district of Bihar, on a high platform in the middle of a pond. Sher Shah died after being injured during the Kalinjar war (1545 A.D.).

questions.q: Zabti system was introduced by –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Zabti was an important system of revenue assessment in the Mughal period. According to major historical sources and Abu’l Fazl’s account, this system is considered to have begun in Sher Shah’s period, while during Akbar’s reign several changes were made to it and it was made more scientific. In Akbar’s time, the Zabti system later became the basis of the “Ain-e-Dahsala.”

questions.q: No government, not even the English, showed as much wisdom as this Pathan did.” Who wrote these words about Sher Shah Suri?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above / More than one of the above

questions.explanation: H. G. Keene wrote about Sher Shah Suri: “No government, not even the English, showed as much wisdom as this Pathan did.” In fact, Keene made this remark in the context of Sher Shah’s administrative/governance system—maintenance of peace and order, roads, sarais (rest houses), the postal system, and other reforms.

questions.q: Where was the battle fought between Sher Shah and Humayun on June 26, 1539?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: The Battle of Chausa was fought in 1539 between Sher Shah Suri and the Mughal ruler Humayun. Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun and assumed the title ‘Farid al-Din Sher Shah’.

questions.q: "After uniting India, he wanted to unite the Mid-East and Western Asia with him as a very important step towards the establishment of a world empire." R. P. Tripathi wrote it about which ruler of Mughal India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above / More than one of the above

questions.explanation: R.P. Tripathi wrote about the Mughal emperor Akbar that “after the unification of India, he wanted to unify the Middle East and Western Asia, which was an important step towards establishing a world empire.”

questions.q: The famous Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri forms which entrance to the Jama Masjid?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The famous Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri serves as the southern entrance of the Jama Masjid. The Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was built by the Mughal ruler Akbar.

questions.q: Who was the commander of Rana Pratap’s army in the Battle of Haldighati?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The Battle of Haldighati was fought in June, 1576 between Maharana Pratap and the Mughal commanders Man Singh and Asaf Khan. Besides the Rajput warriors, the vanguard of Rana’s army was led by Hakim Khan Sur, along with a contingent of Afghans. A small unit of Bhil warriors was also part of Rana’s army. This was Rana’s last direct confrontation with the Mughals; afterwards, he adopted guerrilla warfare.

questions.q: Who of the following Muslim rulers abolished the pilgrimage tax?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The credit for establishing the Mughal administrative system mainly goes to Akbar. His central administration; the explanation of the emperor’s position, powers, and duties; his provincial administration; his revenue system; his currency system; and his mansabdari system all achieved success in his time and became the foundation for his successors. Akbar was the first Muslim emperor who adopted Hindu–Muslim unity and religious tolerance as a political ideal through a well-organzed and declared policy (Sulh-ikul). Under his liberal religious policy, he abolished the slavery system in 1562, the pilgrimage tax in 1563, and the jizya in 1564. As part of social reforms, he also tried to curb child marriage and the practice of sati. Hence, the above four points are included among the reasons for Akbar’s popularity.

questions.q: Akbar merged Bengal and Bihar in to his empire :
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: After Suleiman’s death in 1572, his son Daud Khan ascended the throne. Daud Khan declared himself independent and attacked the Mughal fort at Patna. Akbar ordered Munim Khan to attack Daud and conquer Bihar. Munim Khan defeated Daud in a battle, and by 1574, Mughal authority was established over Bihar. After the defeat, Daud fled to Bengal; however, on 12 July, 1576, in the Battle of Rajmahal, Todar Mal, Muzaffar Khan, and Husain Quli together defeated Daud completely. Thus, in 1576, Bengal and Bihar were fully annexed into the Mughal Empire.

questions.q: Who promulgated Din-e-Elahi?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In 1582, Akbar established ‘Tauhid-i-Ilahi’ or ‘Din-i-Ilahi’. Under it, Akbar tried to include the core principles of all religions and make it universally acceptable. Din-i-Ilahi was essentially a system of thought based on Sufi pantheism. Its chief priest was Abul Fazl. Among Hindus, only Birbal accepted it.

questions.q: During the time of which Mughal Emperor did Sir Thomas Roe come to India?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: William Hawkins (1608-1611 A.D.) was the first English ambassador sent by the East India Company to Jahangir’s court, and the first Englishman to appear at the Mughal court as a representative of the Company. Emperor Jahangir granted him a mansab of 400. He conferred on Hawkins the title of ‘English Khan’ and arranged his marriage with an Armenian woman. Sir Thomas Roe was the first ambassador sent by King James I, who came to Jahangir’s court.

questions.q: Whom of the following Englishmen did Jahangir honour with the title ‘English Khan’?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: William Hawkins (1608-1611 A.D.) was the first English ambassador sent by the East India Company to Jahangir’s court, and the first Englishman to appear at the Mughal court as a representative of the Company. Emperor Jahangir granted him a mansab of 400. He conferred on Hawkins the title of ‘English Khan’ and arranged his marriage with an Armenian woman. Sir Thomas Roe was the first ambassador sent by King James I, who came to Jahangir’s court.

questions.q: Itimad-ud-Daulah’s tomb at Agra was built by
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah was built by Nur Jahan between 1622-28 A.D., after the death of her father. It is a highly ornate building situated on the bank of the Yamuna River in Agra. This quadrangular tomb is the first Mughalperiod tomb in which marble was used on a large scale, and for decoration, the pietra dura technique was used—probably for the first time in Islamic buildings.

questions.q: Pachchikari/Parchinkari (Pietra dura) is related to which of the following?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Decorating the walls with floral designs made of semiprecious stones
options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pachchikari/Parchinkari (pietra dura) is related to making floral designs by inlaying semi-precious stones into walls. It should be noted that in India, pietra dura inlay work was first carried out in the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah. This tomb was built by Nur Jahan, the wife of Jahangir.

questions.q: Who built the Red Fort in Delhi?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Like Akbar’s Fatehpur Sikri, Shah Jahan founded a city in Delhi in his own name called ‘Shahjahanabad’ in 1638 A.D., and tried to adorn it by constructing many beautiful and magnificent buildings. Among the buildings of Shahjahanabad, the Red Fort is the most prominent. This fort is of an irregular octagonal shape and is called the Red Fort because it is built of red sandstone. Its construction began in 1639 A.D. and was completed in about nine years. The western gate of the fort is called the Lahori Gate, and the southern gate is called the Delhi Gate. It is unique in beauty and splendour and is perhaps incomparable in the world.

questions.q: Who among the following historians declared the regime of Shah Jahan to be the Golden Era of the Mughal period?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Dr. A. L. Shrivastava wrote in his book Mughal India that Shah Jahan’s reign is famous as the ‘Golden Age’ in the medieval history of India. This can be considered true only in the sphere of art—particularly architecture. J. N. Sarkar and V. A. Smith do not consider Shah Jahan’s period as a golden age. S. R. Sharma clearly regarded Shah Jahan’s period as the golden age of the Mughal era. Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.q: What was the root of the dispute between the Shah of Iran and Mughal rulers?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Qandahar (Kandahar) was the root of the conflict between the Shah of Iran and the Mughals, because keeping Qandahar under one’s control became a matter of strategic importance, economic interest, as well as emotion and prestige for both the Mughal rulers and the Shah of Iran. The implementation of the imperial plans of both rulers largely depended on holding Qandahar under their control.

questions.q: The meaning of ‘Jihad’ carried on by Aurangzeb is –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Aurangzeb was, above all, a zealous Sunni Muslim. His religious policy was not influenced by any idea of worldly gain. Having obtained the throne as a supporter of Sunni orthodoxy against the liberal Dara, he tried to enforce the law of the Quran strictly. According to this law, every devout Muslim should “strive in the path of Allah,” or in other words, should continue jihad against non-Muslim countries (Darul-Harb) until they are transformed into the domain of Islam (Dar-ul-Islam).

questions.q: Who was the first Mughal ruler who fought against the British?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The first conflict of the Mughals with the English (British) took place in 1686 A.D. during the reign of Aurangzeb. The Mughal governor Shaista Khan drove out the English, including Job Charnock, from Hugli (Hooghly).

questions.q: The meaning of the word Bantai during the Medieval period was?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: In the medieval period, the term Bantai referred to a method of revenue assessment in which the actual produce was divided between the state and the cultivator. Sher Shah Suri adopted three systems for revenue assessment—(1) Nashq or Muqta‘i or Kanqut, (2) Cash assessment or Zabti, and (3) Galla Bakhshi or Batai (Bantai). Bantai was of three types— (1) Khet Batai, (2) Lang Batai, and (3) Ras Batai.

questions.q: Who introduced ‘Do-aspa and Sih-aspa’ system?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The ‘Do-Aspa and Sih-Aspa’ system was introduced by Jahangir. Under it, mansabdars had to maintain a larger force without any increase in their zat rank. (i) Do-Aspa—In this, mansabdars had to keep horses double the number of their ‘sawar’ rank. (ii) Sih-Aspa—In this, mansabdars had to keep horses three times the number of their sawar rank.

questions.q: In the Mughal administration ‘Muhtasib’ was –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: In administration, the Muhtasib was the officer of the department for inspection of public conduct. His duty was to maintain high moral standards among the people. To keep public conduct pure, Akbar imposed restrictions on the open and uncontrolled trade of liquor and prohibited prostitutes from residing in cities. Prostitutes were expelled from the city and settled at a new place, which was named ‘Shaitanpuri’.

questions.q: ‘Madad-e-Mash’ indicates in Mughal administration –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.B: Revenue free land granted to a learned person

questions.explanation: In the Mughal administration, the revenue-free grant of land given to scholars and religious persons was called ‘Madade-Maash’. It was also known as ‘Suyurghal’. The inspection of all donated lands was done by the Sadr, and it was also the Sadr’s responsibility to ensure that these grants were not misused. This land was non-transferable, and it remained with the grantee on a hereditary basis.

questions.q: In Mughal administration, the 'Chief Qazi' was -
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The ‘Chief Qazi’ (Qazi-ul-Quzat) was the principal Qazi and the head of the judicial department.

questions.q: In medieval India, why was the mansabdari system introduced?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Mansabdari system was a special administrative system introduced by the Mughal ruler Akbar. A mansab determined three things—(1) the officer’s order of precedence, (2) the pay scale, and (3) military responsibility. Under military responsibility, a mansabdar had to maintain soldiers according to his mansab. Through this system, the state placed the direct responsibility of recruitment and maintenance of soldiers upon the mansabdars, in return for which the mansabdar was granted cash or a jagir.

chapters.chapter_name: Music and Painting of the Mughal Period

questions.q: Which Mughal ruler established Karkhanas for painting?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Humayun had a painting workshop (Nigar-khana / Tasvirkhana) set up, which was connected to his library. questions.q: Mughal painting reached its zenith under –

questions.explanation: Mughal painting reached its peak during Jahangir’s reign. Jahangir was a highly skilled connoisseur of painting. In the Mughal style, while painting human figures, it was common that in the same painting different painters painted the face, the body and the legs. Jahangir claimed that he could identify the separate contributions of different painters in any painting. Besides painting hunting, war and royal court scenes, there was special progress during Jahangir’s reign in the art of painting humans and animals. Abul Hasan made a painting of Jahangir’s coronation, which was placed on the main page of Jahangir’s autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Jahangir’s period is called the Golden Age of Mughal painting.

Therefore, many people began writing history, and Gulbadan’s Humayun-nama was also written according to this order.

questions.q: Futuhat-i-Alamgiri was written by
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: The book Futuhat-i-Alamgiri was written by Ishwardas Nagar, who served as a Mughal officer in the Jodhpur region for a long time. This work includes some important events of Aurangzeb’s reign (up to A.D. 1698). It also throws considerable light on provincial administration in Malwa and Rajputana. It contains deep insights into some of the mysteries surrounding his reign; however, the work has at times been portrayed as biased, orthodox, communal, sectarian, and even anti-people. It is noteworthy that in Futuhat-i-Alamgiri, the emperor is shown neither as a supporter of Islam nor as a persecutor of Hinduism. Moreover, neither the conflict with Shivaji nor the events after the death of Jaswant Singh are presented from a religious perspective.

Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan translated it into Persian, while the first English translation of Baburnama was done by John Leyden and William Erskine.

questions.q: Which among the following ports was called Bab-ul -Makkah (Gate of Makkah) during the Mughal period?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: During the Mughal period, Surat was called Bab-ul-Makkah (Gateway to Makkah) because the pilgrimage to Makkah began from Surat. Surat is a major city of Gujarat. It is known for its textiles and is one of the main centres of diamond cutting and polishing. In world history, during the medieval period, it was an important port. It was known as the Gateway to Makkah because many travellers used to depart from Surat by sea route. It was also known as a gateway to West Asia, because Surat was one of the major centres for goods and textiles traded with other Asian countries through sea routes.

questions.q: 'Ashta Pradhan' was helping in the Administration of which ruler?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: For the administration of the Maratha state, Shivaji created the Ashtapradhan system at the central level, under which eight ministers were appointed. These included Peshwa, Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Panditrao, and Nyayadhish. They functioned like modern-day secretaries in Shivaji’s administration. Their role was only to advise the king. It cannot be called a council of ministers in the real sense. Each minister was responsible to the king. Details are as follows— (i) Peshwa – Prime Minister of the king. (ii) Amatya or Mazumdar – Minister of Finance and Revenue. (iii) Waqia Navis or Mantri – Kept records of the king’s daily work and the day-to-day proceedings of the court. (iv) Sachiv or Shurunavis – Looked after official correspondence. (v) Sumant or Dabir – Foreign Minister. (vi) Senapati or Sar-e-Naubat – Managed recruitment, organization, supplies, etc., of the army. (vii) Panditrao – Responsible for grants to scholars and for religious works. (viii) Nyayadhish – Chief Justice.

questions.q: Which of the following Mughal emperors was not allowed to enter into Delhi by Wazir Ghaziuddin?
questions.question_type: Negative/Exception MCQ — Single Correct
questions.explanation: The reign of Shah Alam II lasted from 1759 to 1806. His real name was Ali Gauhar. At the time of his father Alamgir II’s death, he was in Bihar. Although he was declared the Mughal emperor, due to factionalism in the Mughal court, he remained outside Delhi, and the throne of Delhi remained vacant from 1760 to 1771. In 1772, he could reach Delhi only with the help of the Marathas. During Shah Alam II’s time, the British captured Delhi (1803).
